section_summary: This section concludes a list of Japanese Diet members arrested or indicted, then presents Despatch No. 413 and the English and Japanese texts of the Supreme Court’s judgment in the Nishio Suehiro political-contributions and perjury case. The Court upheld Nishio’s acquittal on the political-finance charge, while holding that the perjury prosecution was procedurally invalid without an accusation from the Diet; two justices dissented over whether the contractors’ donation was really made to Nishio or to the Social Democratic Party. The remainder contains a detailed report on the creation of the Ministry of International Trade and Industry and the opening portion of its Establishment Law, covering the ministry’s powers, bureaus, inspection offices, regional administration, and Resources Agency.

subfiles.title: Sub-enclosure: Diet Members Indicted or Arrested—Other Cases
subfiles.about: Continuation of a table listing criminal accusations against members of the Japanese House of Representatives and House of Councillors.
subfiles.summary: Table of Diet members indicted or arrested in other cases, from commodity-control violations to fraud, bribery and perjury; Hara Susumu and Asai Ichiro were acquitted.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 413: Supreme Court Judgment in the Nishio Case
subfiles.from: Cloyce K. Huston, Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Office of the United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports the Supreme Court of Japan’s decision in Nishio Suehiro’s political-contribution and perjury case.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 413: the Supreme Court upheld Nishio's acquittal on contribution reporting and dismissed perjury; the dissent and the ruling's relaxed test may affect the Showa Denko trials of Nishio and Ashida.

subfiles.title: English Translation of the Supreme Court Judgment in the Nishio Case
subfiles.from: Grand Bench, Supreme Court of Japan
subfiles.about: English translation of the Supreme Court judgment resolving the government’s appeal in the Nishio case.
subfiles.summary: The majority holds that the reporting duty under Cabinet Ordinance No. 328 of 1947 applied only when financial aid was understood by the recipient to have been given to a political party; because the trial court accepted Nishio’s claim that he received the ¥500,000 personally for discretionary support of the party’s right wing, his acquittal on that count stood. The Court nevertheless quashes the disposition of the perjury count, reasoning that prosecution required an accusation by the House of Representatives or its committee. Justices Mano and Iwamatsu dissent on the contribution issue, arguing that a conditional donation can still be a party donation and that the contractors’ evidence showed the money was intended to benefit the Social Democratic Party while excluding its left wing.

subfiles.title: Japanese Text of the Supreme Court Judgment in the Nishio Case
subfiles.from: Grand Bench, Supreme Court of Japan
subfiles.about: Japanese-language original of the Supreme Court judgment supplied with Despatch No. 413.
subfiles.summary: This enclosure reproduces in Japanese the judgment translated in the preceding enclosure. It addresses Nishio’s receipt of contractors’ funds, the distinction between a personal and party donation, and the procedural requirement for prosecuting perjury before a Diet committee. The concluding pages identify the participating procurators and Supreme Court justices and date the decision June 1, 1949.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 489: Organization and Functions of the Ministry of International Trade and Industry
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, Office of the United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Analyzes the structure, functions, personnel, and likely administrative problems of Japan’s newly created Ministry of International Trade and Industry.
subfiles.summary: The despatch reports that the new ministry combined the former Board of Trade with the Ministry of Commerce and Industry as part of Japan’s export-oriented economic stabilization program. It outlines the ministry’s eight bureaus, inspection offices, regional branches, external agencies, government corporations, and planned twenty-percent personnel reduction. The analysis warns of overlapping jurisdictions, excessive bureaucratic duplication, possible patronage positions, and rivalry between former Board of Trade personnel and officials of the old ministry. Sebald concludes that there was little evidence that abolishing the Board of Trade had eliminated the cumbersome procedures associated with it.

subfiles.title: Ministry of International Trade and Industry Establishment Law, Law No. 102 of 1949
subfiles.about: Opening portion of the English translation of the law establishing the Ministry of International Trade and Industry and defining its organization and powers.
subfiles.summary: The statute establishes the ministry, enumerates its broad authority over international trade, foreign exchange, industrial production, distribution, mining, electric power, industrial property, standards, research, and state alcohol sales, and assigns functions to eight internal bureaus. It creates inspection houses, advisory councils, regional bureaus, and local offices, listing their locations and areas of jurisdiction. The excerpt then begins the provisions for external organs, especially the Resources Agency and its coal, mining, mine-safety, and electric-power bureaus. The law continues beyond page 386 of this section.
